item.processing: Arc-melting pure metals, TiN, and TiO2; remelted at least eight times; drop-cast into water-cooled copper mold
item.test_conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10^-3 s^-1); Damping measured at 1.0 Hz, 300-1100 K
item.structure_change: Formation of ordered oxygen complexes (OOCs) and compositional clusters; single-phase bcc structure retained
item.property_change: Yield strength increased from ~810 MPa to ~1138 MPa; elongation doubled from ~10.8% to ~20%; tanδ_max increased from 0.014 to 0.020
item.attributed_mechanism: Ordered interstitial complexes provide high strain hardening; randomly distributed oxygen atoms enhance damping
quotes: The interstitial doped HEAs have a strong solid-solution strengthening, i.e., the yield strength was increased to 1138 and 1362 MPa for the O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.
Particularly, the ductility of the O-2 HEA was unexpectedly doubled, which has been earlier associated with the formation of ordered interstitial complexes that provide high strain hardening.
The addition of oxygen or nitrogen effectively further enhances the damping capacity, and the tanδ max value at 1.0 Hz of the O-2 and N-2 HEAs increases to 0.020 and 0.027, respectively.

item.test_conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10^-3 s^-1); Damping measured at 1.0 Hz, 300-1100 K

item.property_change: Yield strength increased from ~810 MPa to ~1362 MPa; elongation retained at ~11.9%; tanδ_max increased from 0.014 to 0.027
item.attributed_mechanism: Larger atomic size of nitrogen leads to higher strengthening; ~94.7% of nitrogen atoms are randomly distributed favoring damping
quotes: The interstitial doped HEAs have a strong solid-solution strengthening, i.e., the yield strength was increased to 1138 and 1362 MPa for the O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.
Interstitial reinforcement by nitrogen is more effective than that conveyed by oxygen doping.
As a result, the N-2 HEA exhibits both improved tensile yield strength (σ y ~ 1362 MPa) and damping properties (tanδ max ~ 0.027 at 1.0 Hz).

item.intervention: Increase in vibration frequency from 1.0 Hz to 4.0 Hz
item.processing: Forced vibration on multifunction internal friction apparatus
item.test_conditions: Temperature range 300-1100 K; heating rate 2 K min^-1; max strain amplitude 2 × 10^-4
item.structure_change: No structural change; thermally activated relaxation peaks shift
item.property_change: Peak temperature (T_p) increases while peak height (tanδ_max) decreases
item.attributed_mechanism: Thermally activated relaxation process characteristic of Snoek damping
quotes: The data also reveal that the relaxation peaks are thermally activated since the peak temperature increases while the peak height (i.e., tanδ max ) decreases with increasing vibration frequency.
Such a frequency-dependent damping behavior is characteristic of strain relaxation damping, i.e., Snoek damping.
The measurements were conducted on a multifunction internal friction apparatus by the forced vibration at 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 4.0 Hz, respectively.

item.intervention: Trace oxygen contamination (0.377 at %) from fabrication
item.processing: Arc-melting and drop-casting in argon atmosphere
item.structure_change: Presence of randomly distributed interstitial atoms (impurities)
item.property_change: Exhibits Snoek-type damping behavior with tanδ_max of 0.014
item.attributed_mechanism: Trace oxygen from fabrication process causes Snoek-type damping
quotes: It should be noted that even in the base HEA, the level of oxygen is 0.377 at %, resulting from the fabrication process.
The base HEA used as reference material also shows a Snoek-type damping behavior, which might be due to the trace oxygen contamination from the fabrication process.
Specifically at 1.0 Hz, the tanδ max of the reference HEA Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi reaches a high damping value of 0.014.

item.structure_change: Appearance of additional low-temperature damping peak at 577 K due to ordered oxygen complexes
item.property_change: Additional low-temperature peak height of 0.005; total tanδ_max increases to 0.020
item.attributed_mechanism: Formation of ordered oxygen complexes gives rise to the additional low-temperature peak
quotes: Moreover, in addition to a main damping peak at high temperature, a distinct additional damping peak at low temperature (see white arrows in Fig. 1, B and C ) was observed in the O-2 and N-2 HEAs.
In the material with 2.0 at % oxygen, i.e., in the O-2 HEA, a low-temperature peak (red curve in Fig. 5B ) appears at 577 K, in addition to the two high-temperature peaks.
The formation of ordered oxygen complexes gives rise to the additional low-temperature peak.

item.structure_change: Appearance of additional low-temperature damping peak due to ordered nitrogen complexes
item.property_change: Additional low-temperature peak height of 0.002; total tanδ_max increases to 0.027
item.attributed_mechanism: Ordered nitrogen complexes contribute to the additional peak, though at lower frequency than oxygen
quotes: Unexpectedly, we also observed ordered nitrogen complexes in the N-2 material (see fig. S1), although at a much smaller frequency compared to the oxygen clusters observed in the O-2 alloy.
For the nitrogen-doped N-2 HEA, an additional low-temperature peak (blue curve) and two high-temperature peaks (green and magenta curves) were also observed.
The peak height of the additional low-temperature peak is 0.002, and that of the two high-temperature peaks is 0.027 and 0.009, respectively.

item.structure_change: Activation energy for interstitial reorientation increases
item.property_change: Activation energy H estimated at 2.40 eV (vs 2.06 eV for base)
item.attributed_mechanism: Nitrogen atoms switch positions at higher barriers than oxygen; oxygen in O-2 has intermediate barrier
quotes: The activation energy H is estimated to be 2.06, 2.40, and 4.06 eV for the reference alloy and the interstitially doped O-2 and N-2 HEAs, respectively.

The activation energy H of the N-2 HEA is much higher than that of the base and O-2 HEA, implying that the nitrogen atoms switch their positions at higher barriers than oxygen in the Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi HEA matrix.
To obtain the activation energy H associated with specific stress-induced reorientation mechanisms of the interstitial atoms, we conducted an Arrhenius analysis.

item.structure_change: Ordered oxygen complexes form, consuming ~18.5% of oxygen atoms
item.property_change: Ductility doubles to ~20%; damping capacity increases
item.attributed_mechanism: Ordered interstitial complexes enable enhanced ductility via strain hardening
quotes: Moreover, as estimated by the ratio between the peak height of the additional peak and the total peak height, ~18.5% of all the oxygen atoms in the O-2 HEA participate in the formation of ordered oxygen complexes, enabling the enhanced ductility of this material.
The addition of either oxygen or nitrogen to the base HEA did not appreciably deteriorate the work hardening behavior.
The interstitial doped HEAs retain the same level of ductility but display 70 to 105% higher yield strength than Ti-25Nb-1.5O alloy.

item.structure_change: Only ~5.3% of nitrogen atoms form ordered complexes; most remain randomly distributed
item.property_change: Strongest damping peak (tanδ_max ~ 0.027) among all HEAs; yield strength ~1362 MPa
item.attributed_mechanism: Randomly distributed interstitial atoms improve mechanical damping; limited ordered complexes do not deteriorate ductility
quotes: Hence, only ~5.3% of all the nitrogen atoms in the N-2 HEA contribute to the formation of ordered nitrogen complexes.
As most of the nitrogen is interstitially randomly distributed, the N-2 HEA shows the strongest damping peak among all three HEAs studied here.
The ductility of the N-2 HEA (~11.9%) was not obviously deteriorated because of the formation of the limited ordered nitrogen complexes, in comparison to the base HEA.

item.test_conditions: STEM-ABF and Atom Probe Tomography analysis
item.structure_change: Oxygen occupies interstitial sites adjacent to light atoms (Zr, Ti); formation of O-rich clusters
item.property_change: Not directly measured as property change, but linked to structural origin of properties
item.attributed_mechanism: Oxygen tends to prefer interstitial positions adjacent to lattice sites occupied by light atoms
quotes: The aberration-corrected STEM-ABF (annular bright field) image ( Fig. 4G ) reveals that oxygen occupies the interstitial sites in the bcc lattice.

Furthermore, statistical analysis of the STEM-HAADF and the corresponding ABF images ( Fig. 4, F and G ) confirm that oxygen tends to prefer interstitial positions adjacent to lattice sites, which are occupied by light atoms (i.e., Zr and/or Ti), accumulating to the so-called ordered oxygen complexes.
In Fig. 4H , a set of cyan-colored isocomposition surfaces reveals regions containing more than 3.5 at % O, showing the presence of O-rich clusters.

item.structure_change: Single-phase bcc structure with randomly distributed nitrogen
item.property_change: Peak capacity of damping as high as 0.030 at 0.5 Hz; energy dissipation ~18.8% per cycle
item.attributed_mechanism: High configurational variety of interstitial relaxation processes leads to broadened peaks
quotes: In addition, the peak capacity of damping is as high as 0.030 for the N-2 HEA at 0.5 Hz, which corresponds to an energy dissipation of about 18.8% in each vibrational load cycle.
The highest peak temperature (~800 K) attained so far renders the current interstitial-alloyed HEAs suited for high-temperature damping applications.
This mechanism leads to strongly broadened Snoek-type peaks.

item.intervention: Addition of interstitial atoms (O or N) to HEA matrix
item.structure_change: Severely distorted lattices with complex chemical short-range orders
item.property_change: Peak temperature of damping ~100 K higher than traditional alloys; high activation barrier energies
item.attributed_mechanism: High configuration entropy and distorted lattices impede atomic position switches of interstitials
quotes: It is also important to note that the peak temperature of damping in the current Snoek-type high-damping HEAs is approximately 100 K higher than that in traditional high-damping alloys.
This effect gives rise to the high activation temperatures and barrier energies for the interstitial reorientation steps and the resulting high-temperature damping capability.
